nodes.title: Basic electrical principles
nodes.why: To understand and work with sensor wiring, power supplies, and communication loops on equipment.
checkpoints: Voltage is the electrical potential difference between two points.
Current flows from higher to lower potential, measured in amperes.
Resistance opposes current flow, determined by material and geometry.
Ohm's law relates voltage, current, and resistance, because V = I * R.

nodes.title: Instrumentation fundamentals
nodes.why: To select, configure, and calibrate field instruments that measure process variables.
checkpoints: A sensor converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal.
Signal conditioning amplifies or scales raw sensor output to usable ranges.
Calibration aligns a sensor's output with known reference values.
Transducers often output a standardized current, such as 4-20 mA, for industrial communication.

nodes.title: Basic safety practices
nodes.why: To perform work safely by isolating energy sources and protecting against falls and arc hazards.
checkpoints: Lockout/tagout isolates energy sources before work, preventing accidental startup.
Fall protection equipment must be anchored to a sturdy point, because fall forces are transferred there.
Arc flash hazards require insulated tools and appropriate PPE to avoid burns.
Personal protective equipment is selected based on the identified hazard category.

nodes.title: Control systems basics
nodes.why: To monitor and control field devices through SCADA and related control loops.
checkpoints: SCADA monitors and controls field devices via remote telemetry.
A control loop consists of sensor, controller, and actuator to maintain a setpoint.
Human-machine interfaces display real-time process data for operators.
Alarms in control systems trigger when measurements exceed defined thresholds, because limits are breached.

nodes.title: Pressure, temperature, and vibration sensor calibration
nodes.why: To ensure pressure, temperature, and vibration sensors provide accurate readings for turbine and substation monitoring.
nodes.quote: Calibrate, troubleshoot and replace pressure, temperature and vibration sensors
checkpoints: Pressure sensors output voltage proportional to pressure, so a higher pressure yields higher voltage.
Temperature sensors like RTDs change resistance with temperature, requiring a Wheatstone bridge for measurement.
Vibration sensors (accelerometers) produce charge proportional to acceleration, which is converted to voltage.
Improper grounding can cause sensor signal noise, leading to false readings during calibration.

nodes.title: 4-20 mA loop tracing
nodes.why: To trace and verify current loops that transmit sensor data to the SCADA system.
checkpoints: A 4-20 mA loop provides a live zero at 4 mA, so a broken wire appears as 0 mA.
Current in a loop is limited by the loop's total resistance and the power supply voltage.
Loop continuity is verified with a clamp meter, because the current can be measured without breaking the circuit.
Increasing loop resistance reduces current, which can cause the sensor to read low values.

nodes.title: Modbus communication troubleshooting
nodes.why: To diagnose communication issues between field devices and SCADA using Modbus protocol.
nodes.quote: Modbus signals from the field device to the SCADA system
checkpoints: Modbus uses a master/slave architecture where the master initiates requests.
Modbus RTU frames include a CRC checksum for error detection.
Addressing errors cause devices to ignore requests, so each slave must have a unique ID.
Baud rate mismatches between devices corrupt communication, leading to timeouts.

nodes.title: P&IDs and electrical schematics interpretation
nodes.why: To interpret drawings that locate instruments and define wiring for maintenance tasks.
nodes.quote: Read and mark up P&IDs, loop diagrams and electrical schematics
checkpoints: P&IDs show process flow and instrumentation symbols, allowing identification of sensor locations.
Loop diagrams connect field devices to control system I/O points, illustrating signal paths.
Electrical schematics use standardized symbols for relays, contacts, and power distribution.
Cross-referencing a P&ID with a schematic reveals wiring changes, because they reference the same tag numbers.

nodes.title: Lockout/tagout procedures
nodes.why: To safely de‑energize equipment before performing calibration or repair work.
checkpoints: Lockout devices physically prevent equipment operation, while tags provide warning information.
Procedures require verification of zero energy before work begins, because residual energy may remain.
Multiple energy sources must be isolated, so each source receives its own lock and tag.
Authorized personnel remove locks only after confirming the equipment is safe, preventing accidental restart.

nodes.title: Working at height safety
nodes.why: To access high-mounted equipment on turbines and substations while preventing falls.
checkpoints: Fall arrest systems stop a fall by deploying a rope at a specific length, limiting descent distance.
Anchorage points must support at least five times the expected load, because forces are amplified during a fall.
Lanyards are inspected for cuts before each use, as damaged lines can fail under load.
Work platforms must be secured to prevent tipping, because unstable platforms increase fall risk.

nodes.title: PLC basics and ladder logic
nodes.why: To read and understand ladder logic programs that control instrumentation and process functions.
nodes.quote: PLC basics, including reading ladder logic
checkpoints: Ladder logic programs consist of rungs that represent Boolean control statements.
Inputs are read as discrete signals, which can be energized or de-energized.
Outputs are energized based on the logical results of the rung evaluations.
Scan cycles read inputs, execute logic, then update outputs, because the PLC processes sequentially.

nodes.title: SCADA trends analysis
nodes.why: To analyze real‑time data trends to predict equipment failures before downtime occurs.
nodes.quote: Use SCADA trends to find failing equipment
checkpoints: Trend logs store historical tag values, enabling analysis of equipment performance over time.
Anomalous upward drift in temperature trends can indicate impending component failure.
SCADA alarms can be suppressed during trend analysis to avoid nuisance alerts.
Predictive alerts are generated when monitored parameters exceed predefined deviation limits, because thresholds are breached.

nodes.title: Maintenance documentation
nodes.why: To record calibration activities and work orders clearly in the maintenance management system.
nodes.quote: Write clear work orders and calibration records
checkpoints: Work orders contain a description of the task, required parts, and assigned personnel.
Calibration records must include date, instrument ID, and measured versus expected values.
Documented actions provide traceability for regulatory compliance and future troubleshooting.
Accurate timestamps in records ensure chronological tracking of maintenance activities.

nodes.title: Renewable energy controller fundamentals
nodes.why: To work with solar inverter and wind turbine controller systems that manage power conversion and turbine operation.
nodes.quote: experience with solar inverters or wind turbine controllers
checkpoints: Solar inverters convert DC from panels to AC, synchronizing output with grid frequency.
Wind turbine controllers regulate blade pitch and generator torque to maintain rated power.
Both systems communicate status via Modbus or similar protocols, allowing SCADA integration.
Controller firmware updates can modify control algorithms, influencing performance and protection settings.
